# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Hypothesis title: Repurposing approved antirheumatic leflunomide (active metabolite teriflunomide) as a differentiation-inducing DHODH inhibitor for cytarabine-resistant, oxidative-metabolism-dependent AML residual disease.

Original indication and verification status. Leflunomide is approved for rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis, and its active metabolite teriflunomide is separately approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis; these approval facts are recalled and are NOT stated in the packet (unverified prior knowledge; confirm against regulatory labels). DHODH-targeted development in AML with non-approved compounds is also prior knowledge needing checking; the novelty claimed here is use of an already-approved oral prodrug, not the target concept. This proposal is not venetoclax-azacitidine or any other established AML regimen, which serve only as comparators [S3].

Biological context and hypothesis statement. The context is post-cytarabine residual disease, which [S2] showed was not consistently enriched for quiescent leukemia stem cells but instead carried mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-linked oxidative-metabolism features and depended on oxidative metabolism. Hypothesis: in this residual oxidative-metabolism state, teriflunomide generated from oral leflunomide will engage DHODH at exposures compatible with approved human dosing, constrict de novo pyrimidine synthesis, and convert the differentiation-blocked residual cells toward myeloid lineage (CD11b/CD14 acquisition) with a functional fall in leukemia-initiating frequency, rather than relying on nonspecific mitochondrial cell killing.

Supported premises (from the packet). (1) [S2] establishes the disease state: cytarabine-resistant residual cells required oxidative metabolism, and perturbing that state changed treatment response. (2) [S4] establishes the mechanistic precedent: DHODH inhibition overcame the differentiation block in experimental AML and affected disease-related endpoints. Note that [S4] used DHODH inhibitors, not leflunomide; extending this to leflunomide/teriflunomide is a bridge, not evidence. (3) [S1] provides the selectivity benchmark: ROS-low quiescent LSCs had elevated BCL-2 and OXPHOS dependency; my endpoints must test whether the differentiation approach affects stem function and spares normal hematopoiesis, without assuming residual disease equals the [S2]-cautioned non-identity with the [S1] ROS-low population. (4) [S3] supplies the established metabolic comparator (venetoclax-azacitidine disrupting LSC energy metabolism) used only for benchmarking arms.

Speculative bridges (explicitly assumed, untested). Bridge A (exposure): unbound teriflunomide levels achievable with approved dosing (recalled pharmacology: high protein binding, long half-life; unverified) will reach DHODH-inhibitory concentrations in marrow blasts. Bridge B (state dependence): because DHODH is electron-transport-coupled, the oxidative residual state of [S2] will show disproportionate reliance on de novo pyrimidine synthesis, giving DHODH inhibition selectivity for that state; this coupling logic is inference. Bridge C (stem-level translation): differentiation induction will reduce functional LSC frequency by limiting dilution, not merely shift surface markers. Bridge D (mechanism purity): differentiation and survival effects will be rescued by uridine, tagging pyrimidine-mediated specificity.

Alternative explanations. (1) Cytotoxic pyrimidine starvation kills bulk blasts, and apparent differentiation is skewing of surviving bulk cells. (2) Off-target biology of teriflunomide (reported kinase/proliferation effects at high concentrations; unverified prior knowledge) drives responses independently of DHODH. (3) Immune-mediated effects in vivo confound xenograft readouts. (4) Any combination benefit reflects cytarabine scheduling rather than DHODH inhibition.

Discriminating preclinical validation strategy. (1) Engagement and specificity: treat a primary AML specimen panel, including ex vivo cytarabine-residual generation modeled on [S2], with teriflunomide across clinically relevant unbound concentrations; quantify orotate/dihydroorotate flux shifts, test uridine rescue, and include a DHODH-overexpression resistance arm. (2) Cell-state and endpoint separation: sort ROS-low versus oxidative ROS-high fractions using functional markers per [S1]; measure differentiation (CD11b/CD14, morphology) versus apoptosis (annexin V/caspase) per fraction, and perform limiting-dilution xenograft assays for LSC frequency, thereby keeping bulk, stem, and differentiation endpoints distinct. (3) Normal-cell comparator: cord-blood and adult CD34+ HSPC viability, myeloid colony formation, and long-term culture to define therapeutic window. (4) Comparator arms: venetoclax-azacitidine per [S3] for metabolic-signature and LSC benchmarks, plus a potent investigational DHODH inhibitor (brequinar; unverified status) as mechanistic positive control. (5) In vivo: cytarabine-primed NSG PDX treated with oral leflunomide dosing bridged by PK to human exposure; endpoints: marrow differentiation markers, LSC frequency, and survival.

Falsifying observation. The proposed drug-mechanism-context relationship is disconfirmed if teriflunomide at unbound concentrations consistent with approved human exposure (i) fails to shift orotate/dihydroorotate flux (no target engagement); (ii) engages DHODH but fails to induce differentiation or reduce LSC frequency in the cytarabine-residual oxidative-state fractions; (iii) depletes normal CD34+ HSPCs comparably to AML cells (no therapeutic window); or (iv) produces effects that are not uridine-rescued and persist despite DHODH overexpression, indicating off-target rather than the proposed DHODH-differentiation mechanism.

Limitations. Exposure may be capped by protein binding, long half-life, and hepatotoxicity/teratogenicity warnings (all unverified prior knowledge). [S4] model endpoints may not generalize across AML genotypes; the [S2] residual state is model-derived and may not match clinical marrow; differentiation endpoints require functional LSC assays rather than marker inference; and murine pyrimidine metabolism may not recapitulate human DHODH dependence.

Ranked proposal:
Repurposing approved antirheumatic leflunomide (active metabolite teriflunomide) as a differentiation-inducing DHODH inhibitor for cytarabine-resistant, oxidative-metabolism-dependent AML residual disease
